Caching is easy to add and hard to operate.
The first version usually looks like this: check Redis, return the value if it exists, otherwise query the database and store the result. That is cache-aside in one sentence. It works, but production systems need more than that.
A real API needs to handle cache stampedes, stale data, conditional HTTP requests, background refresh, Redis failures, and clear invalidation rules. Without those details, caching can make your system faster on a normal day and less reliable during traffic spikes.
In this article, we will build a production-style cache-aside API in .NET with Redis, ETags, stale-while-revalidate behavior, and per-key stampede protection.
The Architecture
We will use four layers:
Controller: handles HTTP, ETag headers, and 304 Not Modified responses.
Query service: owns cache-aside behavior and stale-while-revalidate decisions.
Repository: loads the canonical data from the database.
Background refresh queue: refreshes stale values without blocking user requests.
The key rule: Redis is an optimization. The database remains the source of truth.
